title: Value & Growth
summary: Payments infrastructure grows when customers collect, distribute and explain money more successfully. Its commercial model connects merchant outcomes to transaction volume, billed revenue, active accounts and additional services.
scope: Six offering patterns across merchants, SaaS businesses, platforms, recipients and finance teams. Public prices are dated examples. Sales and growth classifications are assessments. Market scenarios are explicit assumptions, not forecasts or a valuation.

framework.summary: Use the Product-Led Growth lens to align the value metric, buying motion and path to first value. Market sizing and unit economics complement that lens. Compare each growth position with a named alternative for a specific customer segment.

strategies.name: Dominant
strategies.definition: Deliver a materially better job outcome for a materially lower price. This describes a value/price position; it does not mean the provider has the largest market share.

strategies.name: Differentiated
strategies.definition: Serve unmet needs substantially better at a premium that the target segment is willing to pay.

strategies.name: Disruptive
strategies.definition: Offer a simpler, cheaper solution with fewer capabilities to overserved customers or people who could not use the existing alternatives.

evidence.note: Strategy definitions follow ProductLed; their application to these offerings is an assessment.

segments.name: Online payment acceptance
segments.summary: Start with a bounded checkout problem, then expand payment methods, markets and processing volume.
segments.outcome: Convert legitimate purchase intent into successfully collected funds at an acceptable total cost.
segments.valueUnit: Successful payment count and collected payment volume, with fraud and refund outcomes alongside them.
segments.pricingUnit: Percentage of payment value plus a fixed transaction fee; separate charges can apply to additional services.
segments.pricingModel: Standard usage pricing gives small merchants a low commitment entry. Larger merchants negotiate volume, product and geography terms.
segments.valueProof: Use comparable merchant cohorts to measure acceptance, net collected revenue, integration effort and cost per successful collection.

selling.buyers: Founder for a small merchant; payments and finance leadership for an enterprise
selling.rationale: A developer can establish technical fit; enterprise approval still involves commercial, risk and operating requirements.

positioning.alternative: A bespoke gateway integration plus separate payment operations tooling
positioning.rationale: A simple hosted checkout can be disruptive for a small merchant; advanced optimization can be differentiated. A dominant claim needs evidence of both better outcomes and lower price.
conditions: Compare the same payment mix and merchant scale.
Include engineering effort and operational costs in the business case.

activation.firstValue: An eligible merchant completes a real payment and verifies the resulting balance and payout path.
activation.repeatValue: A continuing cohort of successfully collected payments with understood exceptions.
activation.expansion: More transaction volume, payment methods, geographies and optional risk services.
frictions: Distinguishing a successful test from live funds availability

entryOffer.rationale: Use testing to remove integration uncertainty, then start with a small amount of paid live processing.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: Useful for a surrounding software feature; weak as a promise of permanently free payment processing.
entryOffer.trialFit: A bounded software trial or fee credit can reduce entry cost, but its duration or allowance must be explicit.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Test checkout, payment failures and refunds in sandbox; prove collection and reconciliation with an approved live payment.
entryOffer.limits: Eligibility, payment-method support and settlement remain live requirements. Keep processing and optional-product fees visible.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: The first billable live transaction under the agreed price schedule; a successful sandbox request triggers no paid conversion.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed 60-day cohort: merchant organizations reaching a reconciled billable live payment divided by merchant organizations starting an evaluation. Report approval failures and time to settlement separately.

evidence.note: Suggested entry design and measurement window, not a measured conversion benchmark.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

segments.name: Enterprise unified commerce
segments.summary: A coordinated online and store rollout is a buying and operating change across several teams.
segments.outcome: Improve cross-channel conversion while reducing fragmented payment and finance operations.
segments.valueUnit: Collected volume across channels, reliably reconciled stores and merchants, and successful cross-channel service outcomes.
segments.pricingUnit: Transaction charges plus separately priced terminals, services and contract-specific commitments.
segments.pricingModel: An enterprise commercial agreement covers the processing scope; hardware and other products need their own cost treatment.
segments.valueProof: Pilot a defined store and online cohort; measure service completion, reconciled settlement, operating effort and rollout economics.

selling.users: Store, ecommerce, payment and finance operations
selling.buyers: CFO, CIO and commerce leadership, with procurement and risk teams
selling.rationale: Broad rollout and shared financial controls normally require leadership sponsorship, even when engineers first explore the API.

positioning.alternative: Separate online and point-of-sale providers with fragmented customer and settlement data
positioning.rationale: Unified operations are a differentiation hypothesis for merchants with unmet cross-channel needs. A premium must be justified against the actual alternative.
conditions: The merchant values cross-channel outcomes enough to change systems.
Migration, hardware and support costs are included.
Public pricing alone cannot establish a premium or a lower total cost.

activation.entry: Discovery and a coordinated store/online pilot
activation.firstValue: One cross-channel purchase or refund is handled and reconciled end to end.
activation.repeatValue: Daily operations and financial close work across the pilot estate.
activation.expansion: Additional stores, regions, channels and agreed services.
frictions: Settlement, refund and offline exposure handling

entryOffer.rationale: A scoped commercial pilot can test the cross-channel operating model before committing the full store estate.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: A basic POS software tier can work for smaller merchants, as Square illustrates. It does not establish the economics of an enterprise rollout.
entryOffer.trialFit: Useful for software-only features; a short generic trial is a poor substitute for terminal deployment and a reconciled operating cycle.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Propose one store cohort and an online channel, including a purchase, cross-channel refund and finance reconciliation.
entryOffer.limits: Agree pilot duration, terminal and integration costs, support, processing charges and success measures. Adyen’s cited terms do not promise a standard paid pilot.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: A pilot contract starts paid evaluation; a separate rollout agreement expands stores, channels or regions after acceptance.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed measure: signed pilots that enter an agreed wider rollout within 90 days of pilot completion divided by all completed pilots. Track deployment time and rollout contribution alongside the rate.

evidence.note: Proposed enterprise entry design; the Square example is scoped to its public US software plans.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

segments.name: Recurring and usage-based revenue
segments.summary: Revenue teams need a trustworthy path from a pricing contract and usage to billing, collection and accounting.
segments.outcome: Launch monetization changes without losing revenue or making the financial close unreliable.
segments.valueUnit: Correctly billed and collected revenue, recovered renewals and billing operations effort.
segments.pricingUnit: Billing volume, software subscription commitments or contract-specific usage tiers.
segments.pricingModel: Usage fees can grow with billed volume. Committed subscription tiers trade flexibility for price predictability; payment processing remains a separate cost where applicable.
segments.valueProof: Reconcile usage, invoices, collections and accounting outputs on a pilot cohort; distinguish customer growth from an improvement caused by billing software.

selling.rationale: A team can prototype pricing quickly, while migration and accounting policy usually require finance approval.

positioning.alternative: Custom billing code plus manual spreadsheets and disconnected collection tooling
positioning.rationale: Support for complex contracts and trustworthy operations can justify a premium for underserved revenue teams.
conditions: The billing complexity exists in the target cohort.
Value includes avoided leakage and operations effort.
Migration and continuing configuration costs are measured.

activation.entry: Reproduce one pricing contract and sample usage in a test environment
activation.firstValue: Issue and collect a correct live invoice, then reconcile it to source usage and finance records.
activation.repeatValue: Recurring invoices and exceptions remain explainable across billing cycles.
activation.expansion: More products, usage models, legal entities and finance automation.

entryOffer.rationale: Trial the billing workflow; consider an ongoing free analytics or limited software tier when it delivers independent value.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: Plausible for reporting and a deliberately bounded software tier. Keep billable billing volume and payment processing separate.
entryOffer.trialFit: Strong when the buyer can reproduce a contract, validate an invoice and see reconciliation during the evaluation window. Chargebee advertises a trial.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Replay representative usage and billing cycles in test; use an approved live cohort to validate actual collection.
entryOffer.limits: State feature and usage limits, expiry and migration effort. Merchant-configured subscriber trials are different from the merchant’s own billing-platform trial.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: An accepted software plan, paid feature or billable usage under the offer’s terms; a subscriber leaving their own trial is a separate event.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed 90-day cohort: evaluating business accounts that become paying billing accounts and produce a reconciled live invoice divided by all evaluation accounts. Separate free-tier upgrades from timed-trial conversions.

evidence.note: Recommended packaging and cohort definition; confirm each vendor’s trial terms before comparison.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

segments.name: Platform payments and recipient activation
segments.summary: A platform sells a service to merchants or sellers while selecting and operating the underlying payment infrastructure.
segments.outcome: Activate eligible sellers and deliver usable earnings with manageable support and risk costs.
segments.valueUnit: Activated, earning accounts and successfully received payouts; platform payment volume is a complementary scale measure.
segments.pricingUnit: Active connected accounts, payout count or volume, processing fees and platform-defined service charges.
segments.pricingModel: Who controls pricing and pays processing fees depends on the commercial model. Separate infrastructure revenue, platform revenue and seller earnings.
segments.valueProof: Follow a seller cohort through verification, first earning, received payout and repeat activity; include restricted and abandoned accounts.

selling.users: Platform engineers and operations; sellers use the embedded experience
selling.payers: Platform or connected merchant according to the arrangement
selling.rationale: The infrastructure purchase is often negotiated at platform level; many sellers discover the service through their existing platform.

positioning.alternative: A platform-built onboarding, ledger and payout stack assembled from separate providers
positioning.rationale: A coherent onboarding and money-movement service can reduce platform complexity and recipient friction.
conditions: Responsibility for losses and support is understood.
The seller receives usable earnings, not just an account.
Account, payout and optional-service economics are visible to each party.

activation.entry: Platform test integration and a small seller cohort
activation.firstValue: An eligible seller completes verification and receives the first usable payout.
activation.repeatValue: Repeat payouts arrive with understandable statements and timely exception resolution.
activation.expansion: More active sellers and geographies; optional services only where eligible and useful.

entryOffer.rationale: Test the platform integration, then validate one seller cohort before expanding commercial use.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: Developer tools or reporting may be free; onboarding a free platform account does not make real seller processing and payouts free.
entryOffer.trialFit: A small seller cohort can prove operations. Do not let a calendar trial obscure verification work or the first payout cycle.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Exercise onboarding, split payments, failed verification and payout events in test, followed by approved live sellers.
entryOffer.limits: State who pays platform and transaction fees, who supports sellers, and what capabilities are approved. Simulated payouts do not establish receipt of funds.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: The contracted platform fee or first billable connected-account activity; separately track when a seller receives a usable payout.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed 90-day cohort: evaluating platforms with billable live activity and at least one reconciled seller payout divided by all evaluating platforms. Report seller activation and verification completion separately.

evidence.note: Entry design distinguishes the platform buyer from its sellers and payout recipients.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

segments.name: Business treasury and payout operations
segments.summary: Finance adopts an account or payout capability when it improves cash access and control in supported markets.
segments.outcome: Make cash usable where it is needed and maintain an explained, reconciled cash position.
segments.valueUnit: Available funds, successful transfers, time to usable cash and reconciled account activity.
segments.pricingUnit: Service-specific account, transfer, FX or card economics; an account balance itself is not provider revenue.
segments.pricingModel: Model explicit service charges and any permitted retained income separately. Availability, pricing and responsibilities vary by product, country and customer eligibility.
segments.valueProof: Run a bounded account and payout pilot; compare cash availability, transfer costs, exception handling and close effort.

selling.payers: The business or platform contracting for the service
channels: Platform distribution for eligible business accounts
selling.rationale: Account controls, permitted use and reconciliation make this a finance-led buying decision even when setup has a self-service interface.

positioning.alternative: Separate banking, payout and reconciliation workflows
positioning.rationale: Connected payment and cash operations may improve control and reduce work for customers with fragmented processes.
conditions: The relevant account capabilities are available to the legal entity.
Total transfer and FX costs justify the change.
Controls and reconciliation meet the customer’s requirements.

activation.entry: Review eligibility and controls, then fund a limited pilot
activation.firstValue: A real transfer reaches its destination and the account activity reconciles.
activation.repeatValue: Recurring funding and payout cycles stay within controls and reconcile without unexplained balances.
activation.expansion: Additional supported entities, currencies or optional financial services.
frictions: Funding, transfer cutoffs and liquidity management

entryOffer.rationale: Demonstrate controls in test, then use a bounded commercial rollout to verify actual funding and transfers.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: Potentially suitable for read-only visibility or software controls. It does not imply free live transfers, FX or financial services.
entryOffer.trialFit: Useful for workflow evaluation; assess live eligibility, approvals and reconciliation independently of any free-access deadline.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Propose one entity, an agreed funding amount and a small transfer set with approvals and reconciled account activity.
entryOffer.limits: Confirm country and product eligibility, transfer fees and limits, FX, support and rollout terms. No standard free treasury trial is established by the cited sources.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: The first contracted service fee or billable transfer after approval; account creation or a simulated balance is not conversion.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed 90-day cohort: evaluating organizations with a reconciled live transfer and billable service use divided by all evaluating organizations. Also measure repeat funding cycles and exceptions.

evidence.note: Proposed evaluation design and measurement window, subject to the selected product’s commercial terms.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

segments.name: Managed payments for digital sellers
segments.summary: A digital seller evaluates a merchant-of-record service against operating payments and indirect-tax processes itself.
segments.outcome: Sell eligible digital products across markets with a manageable operational and compliance burden.
segments.valueUnit: Completed digital sales and collected seller proceeds; time and work required to support the selling model.
segments.pricingUnit: A percentage of the sale plus a fixed transaction amount, with a broader service bundle than standalone processing.
segments.pricingModel: The merchant-of-record agreement defines the sales relationship and responsibilities. Compare its full bundle with the costs and responsibilities of the seller’s alternative.
segments.valueProof: Reconcile a pilot sale, tax treatment, refund and seller payout; compare retained proceeds and operational work.

selling.buyers: Business leadership and finance, with legal review where needed
selling.payers: The digital seller through agreed fees and settlement terms
selling.rationale: A small seller can start evaluation from the product; material migration and commercial changes need an accountable buyer.

positioning.alternative: A payment processor plus seller-operated tax, billing and support arrangements
positioning.rationale: A broader responsibility bundle can justify a higher transaction fee for sellers with unmet operational needs.
conditions: The product and seller are eligible.
The bundled scope is actually needed.
The fixed fee remains acceptable for the average transaction size.

activation.entry: Create a product and test checkout, then obtain required account approval
activation.firstValue: A live digital sale, buyer receipt and seller payout are understood and reconciled.
activation.repeatValue: Renewals, refunds and buyer support work consistently.
activation.expansion: More eligible products, markets and customer volume.

entryOffer.rationale: Let a digital seller validate checkout, then start paid commercial use with an approved product.
entryOffer.freemiumFit: Free analytics can attract sellers, as ProfitWell Metrics shows. It is separate from merchant-of-record processing.
entryOffer.trialFit: Test the seller workflow in sandbox. A free trial offered to the seller’s subscribers does not establish free infrastructure access.
entryOffer.evaluationScope: Test catalog, checkout, renewals and refunds; validate real receipts, commercial responsibilities and seller payout after approval.
entryOffer.limits: Paddle sandbox has no real payouts or monthly statements. Live verification, fees and payout terms need a separate check.
entryOffer.paidTrigger: A billable live sale under the provider’s commercial terms; track the later seller payout as proof of usable value.
entryOffer.conversionMetric: Proposed 90-day cohort: evaluating sellers with an approved product, billable sale and reconciled payout divided by all evaluating sellers. Separate analytics cross-sells from processing activation.

evidence.note: Recommended seller entry model; free analytics and paid processing are separate offers.
Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

benchmarks.name: Stripe online payments
benchmarks.metric: Per successful transaction on standard European cards
benchmarks.caveat: Other card categories, payment methods and services have different fees. This is not the provider’s retained take rate.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

benchmarks.name: Stripe Billing — pay as you go
benchmarks.scope: Includes Billing transactions processed on and off Stripe; excludes one-off invoices.
benchmarks.caveat: Billing is a software fee base; it is not a card-processing rate.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

benchmarks.name: Stripe Billing — committed tier
benchmarks.metric: Up to $100,000 Billing volume per month
benchmarks.scope: Annual subscription paid monthly; displayed additional-volume rate is 0.67%.
benchmarks.caveat: A commitment changes the effective rate at different utilization levels. Check the current quote and separate payment costs.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

benchmarks.name: Stripe Connect — platform handles pricing
benchmarks.metric: Monthly active connected account and payout
benchmarks.scope: Monthly activity is defined by a payout being sent to an external bank account or debit card.
benchmarks.caveat: These fees belong to the platform-handles-pricing model; the Stripe-handles-pricing option has a different structure.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

benchmarks.name: Adyen payment acceptance
benchmarks.metric: Processing activity and applicable payment-method charges
benchmarks.scope: Interchange++ distinguishes passed-through costs and provider charges. Other products are priced separately.
benchmarks.caveat: Minimum invoices depend on industry or business model. Use an agreed merchant-specific quote for numeric comparisons.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

benchmarks.name: Paddle merchant of record
benchmarks.geography: Published standard offer; eligible sellers and products
benchmarks.scope: Bundled payments, billing, tax compliance and related services under the merchant-of-record arrangement.
benchmarks.caveat: A broader responsibility bundle makes a direct comparison with a processor-only fee misleading; the fixed component matters for small tickets.

evidence.note: Public list-price example checked on the stated date.

providers.name: Adyen — commercial depth and enterprise adoption
providers.summary: Adyen illustrates product capability supporting a relationship-led enterprise sale and a platform distribution model. These are segment-specific interpretations, not a blanket claim that every Adyen offering has one growth strategy.

points.label: Value proposition
points.text: Unified Commerce connects online and in-person payment data and experiences. The business case should quantify conversion, operating effort and reconciliation benefits for the particular merchant.

points.label: Buying and onboarding
points.text: Adyen for Platforms describes an assisted path from initial contact to test integration and go-live. Model commercial selection, technical proof and operational readiness as separate gates.

points.label: Revenue mechanism
points.text: Separate processing charges, payment-method components and additional product fees. An invoice can include pass-through costs; the customer’s total fee is not automatically Adyen net revenue.

points.label: Pricing and scale
points.text: The UK pricing page describes minimum invoices by industry or business model. Contract economics and rollout effort should be evaluated for the target merchant size.

points.label: Growth position
points.text: Differentiation is a hypothesis for enterprises with unmet cross-channel needs. Calling Adyen dominant would additionally require evidence of lower price and better outcomes versus a specified alternative.

points.label: Expansion
points.text: Potential expansion includes stores, markets and platform capabilities. Financial-service opportunities depend on eligibility and product availability; attach rate alone is insufficient without customer value.

points.label: Billing and loyalty adjacency
points.text: Adyen announced the July 2026 closing of Orb and Talon.One acquisitions and the start of integration. Treat billing and loyalty expansion as an area to verify at offering level; the announcement does not establish universal integrated availability.

points.label: Decision measures
points.text: Track time from technical proof to first reconciled live cohort, subsequent volume and product expansion, merchant contribution, recipient outcomes and concentration risk.

points.label: Sandbox, trial and pilot distinction
points.text: The documented platform path uses test integration followed by a live application. Treat a bounded paid pilot as a proposed way to prove rollout value, not as an advertised Adyen package. Transaction pricing and possible minimum invoices remain relevant during live evaluation.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

providers.name: Stripe — self-service entry with assisted expansion
providers.summary: Public standard pricing and custom sales paths support a hybrid interpretation. Payments, Billing and Connect also demonstrate that the useful unit of monetization differs across products.

points.label: Entry and sales assistance
points.text: A low-commitment standard offer can attract small teams. Higher volume, product complexity and procurement requirements create reasons for sales and implementation assistance.

points.label: Expansion economics
points.text: Payment volume, billed revenue and active connected accounts are different fee bases. Model expansion by product and avoid adding the same underlying customer spend several times.

points.label: Proof of value
points.text: A test API request validates an integration step. A live collected payment, correct paid invoice or received seller payout is the stronger activation event.

points.label: Whose free trial?
points.text: A Stripe sandbox tests the integration. Billing trial offers govern the merchant’s subscribers. Assess the merchant’s own commercial entry separately: standard payment processing is usage-priced, and other product terms must be checked individually.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

growthLoops.name: Proven collection → merchant expansion
steps: Resolve one merchant collection or reconciliation problem.
Demonstrate repeatable outcomes for the initial cohort.
Expand to additional channels, locations or payment methods.
Use implementation learnings to reduce friction for the next rollout.
signals: Expansion revenue from the same merchant cohort
Time to the next successful rollout
Contribution after support and risk costs
growthLoops.constraint: Merchant growth can increase volume without any product improvement. Separate underlying commerce growth from share gains and product adoption.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

growthLoops.name: Platform adoption → recipient activation → deeper usage
steps: Win a platform with a specific merchant workflow.
Embed verification and payout visibility in that workflow.
Help eligible sellers reach usable earnings.
Expand with platform adoption and recurring seller activity.
growthLoops.constraint: Embedded distribution is not automatically a network effect. Verify that additional participants improve value for others before making that claim.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

growthLoops.name: Trustworthy billing → broader monetization
steps: Support one pricing contract and reconcile the first paid cohort.
Reduce recurring exceptions and manual work.
Introduce another product, price model or eligible market.
Measure retained revenue and continued operational trust.
signals: Revenue retained after contraction and churn
growthLoops.constraint: Increased billings can reflect the customer’s sales growth, price changes or acquisitions; record the cause before attributing it to the infrastructure.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Effective retained take rate
economics.formula: Retained payment-related provider revenue ÷ comparable processed payment volume
economics.measurementCautions: Define the numerator, period and payment scope. A merchant list price includes components that may be passed through; product mix can move the ratio.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Revenue per active merchant or platform
economics.formula: Recognized provider revenue ÷ active contracted customer accounts in the same period
economics.measurementCautions: Define active, use a consistent period and distinguish platforms from their connected sellers. Shopper counts are a different denominator.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Contribution after serving the account
economics.formula: Retained revenue − direct processing, loss, support and delivery costs attributable to the cohort
economics.whyItMatters: Tests whether additional volume improves the business.
economics.measurementCautions: Avoid subtracting pass-through costs twice. Publish the cost allocation and treatment of losses and implementation work.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Acquisition payback
economics.formula: Acquisition and onboarding investment ÷ monthly contribution from the acquired cohort
economics.whyItMatters: Connects selling motion and implementation effort to the time needed to recover investment.
economics.measurementCautions: Use contribution, include implementation effort and allow for ramp time. A simple average is not a discounted lifetime-value estimate.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Net revenue retention
economics.formula: End-period revenue from the starting customer cohort ÷ that cohort’s start-period revenue
economics.whyItMatters: Captures expansion, contraction and churn together.
economics.measurementCautions: Exclude new customers. Separate usage changes, customer commerce growth, price changes and product adoption. Compare the same accounting basis.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Activation and time to usable value
economics.formula: Customers reaching the defined live outcome ÷ eligible starting cohort; time from start to that outcome
economics.whyItMatters: Connects the entry experience to real commercial and customer outcomes.
economics.measurementCautions: Report verification failures, abandonment and time spent waiting. A sandbox event or sent payout is not proof of received funds.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Incremental customer value
economics.formula: Incremental collected contribution + operational savings − incremental product and implementation costs
economics.whyItMatters: Helps the buyer justify the change in terms of its own economics.
economics.measurementCautions: Use a controlled or carefully matched comparison and state uncertainty. Higher authorization alone does not establish incremental profit.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

economics.name: Revenue and volume concentration
economics.formula: Share of retained revenue and payment volume from the largest merchant, platform and sector cohorts
economics.whyItMatters: Makes dependency visible when one platform distributes the service to many sellers.
economics.measurementCautions: A large number of recipient accounts may still depend on a few contracted platforms. Model both levels.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

constraints.title: Eligibility limits the addressable funnel
constraints.description: A signup does not establish access to every payment or financial capability. Segment the funnel by supported entity, country and use case; record verification and approval gates.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

constraints.title: Human assistance is an economic choice
constraints.description: Separate technical setup from the commercial, risk and organizational work required to reach value. For a large merchant, a well-run assisted pilot can be part of the product’s value proposition.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

constraints.title: Recipient trust constrains expansion
constraints.description: Make restrictions, payout state and costs understandable. Optional accounts, cards or financing should have a clear value case and an independent choice; do not treat acceptance of an upsell as payout activation.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

constraints.title: Retention needs an outcome explanation
constraints.description: Integration effort and operational dependence may make switching costly. Measure continued customer outcomes and satisfaction alongside retention, rather than treating difficulty leaving as proof of value.

evidence.note: Commercial interpretation of the cited product and pricing evidence; validate with customer research.

market.summary: A broad payments-industry headline combines activities outside this domain. Start with a bounded customer problem and revenue pool, then estimate the portion a particular offer can serve and win.
market.boundary: The worked scenarios cover remote card acceptance using euro-area card-use data as a demand proxy. They do not estimate the full global TAM of payments and revenue infrastructure.

context.label: Reported card-payment demand
context.description: ECB reports this card-payment value for the euro area. Remote transactions accounted for 30% of card-payment value in that half-year.

evidence.note: Payment value is a demand measure, not payment-provider revenue.

context.label: Why the boundary matters
context.description: The same half-year includes credit transfers and other instruments. Applying a card merchant fee to that entire amount would mix materially different activities.

evidence.note: The aggregate is observed; the warning about monetizing it is analytical.

scenarios.geography: Euro-area remote card-use proxy; merchant acquiring boundaries require reconciliation
scenarios.revenueLabel: Provider revenue per €1 of payment value
assumptions: Proxy volume: €1.8 trillion of H2 2025 card payments × 30% remote share × 2. The last step is an illustrative annualization, not a reported annual total.
The revenue-per-euro input is an assumed effective retained provider rate, including the modeled effect of fixed charges and excluding pass-through network costs.
Serviceable share represents supported countries, legal entities, industries, payment mixes and delivery capacity.
Obtainable share is a three-year scenario input applied to SAM. No market growth is forecast and the output is an annual run rate at that horizon.
limitations: Card-use statistics and merchant acquiring revenue have different reporting boundaries. Reconcile merchant location, cross-border treatment and provider responsibilities before using this as a market estimate.
Annualizing a half-year ignores seasonality; the source values are rounded.
Rates and shares are assumptions, not Adyen or Stripe metrics. Replace them with verified segment economics, pipeline conversion and implementation capacity.

evidence.note: ECB supplies the payment-demand context; annualization, monetization and reachable shares are explicit modeling assumptions.

entryStrategy.summary: Choose an entry offer for the merchant, platform or finance team buying the infrastructure. A trial they offer their own subscribers is a different commercial relationship. Free software, test environments and usage-based live services can coexist. The fit assessments and measurement windows below are proposed designs; provider examples describe publicly documented offers.

models.name: Freemium
models.definition: A useful production software tier remains free without a fixed expiry, while additional capabilities or capacity are paid.
models.bestFit: A recurring software job that users can complete independently and that has an affordable cost to serve.
models.conversion: Upgrade when the customer needs a paid capability, higher limit or broader team access.
models.limits: State the free boundary and underlying payment charges. A temporary credit or one-time allowance is not an unlimited free tier.

models.name: Free trial
models.definition: Access to a defined product or feature set for a limited time without its usual software fee.
models.bestFit: The buyer can reach a meaningful outcome within the evaluation period and understand the later price.
models.conversion: Continue on an explicitly accepted paid plan after proving value; define what happens at expiry.
models.limits: Specify duration, included usage, payment details required and third-party charges. Usage credits have a separate consumption limit.

models.name: Sandbox
models.definition: An isolated environment for testing integrations with simulated payments or financial activity.
models.bestFit: Checkout, billing, platform and payout integrations that need technical verification before launch.
models.conversion: Complete approval and live configuration, then deliver a real, reconciled customer outcome.
models.limits: Successful tests do not prove live eligibility, actual settlement, customer demand or production service economics.

models.name: Paid pilot
models.definition: A proposed bounded commercial engagement to prove value in a real operating setting before a wider rollout.
models.bestFit: Enterprise integrations involving terminals, migration, multiple teams or meaningful implementation work.
models.conversion: Agree success measures, scope, fees and an expansion decision before starting the pilot.
models.limits: A recommendation for a sales design, not a claim that every named provider sells a standard paid-pilot package.

models.name: Pay as you go
models.definition: Live commercial use incurs usage fees; a monthly subscription may be unnecessary.
models.bestFit: A merchant can begin with a small live volume and expand as value grows.
models.conversion: The first billable activity starts paid use; repeat activity demonstrates retention and expansion.
models.limits: No monthly fee does not mean free processing. Minimum invoices, hardware, add-ons and product-specific charges may still apply.

examples.name: Square — free software and timed trials
examples.summary: Square’s US pricing page lists a Free plan without a monthly subscription charge and 30-day free trials for Plus and Premium. Payment processing remains chargeable.
examples.caveat: This is a software-tier example with separate transaction economics. US terms do not establish the same offer in every region or for every enterprise deployment.

evidence.note: Public US pricing and trial terms checked 16 November 2026.

examples.name: Stripe — sandbox, then paid usage
examples.summary: Stripe documents isolated sandboxes; its Belgium standard payments pricing charges per use without a monthly fee. Its Billing trial documentation describes offers a merchant configures for subscribers.
examples.caveat: The subscriber’s trial is separate from the merchant’s commercial terms with Stripe. Sandbox use and no monthly payments fee do not establish a free production tier.

evidence.note: The sandbox, payments price and subscriber-trial documentation describe different parts of the offer.

examples.name: Adyen — technical evaluation and commercial approval
examples.summary: Adyen for Platforms documents contact, implementation scoping, test access and a separate live-account application. Its UK pricing page describes transaction charges and a minimum invoice depending on the business.
examples.caveat: These sources document testing and live commercial terms. They do not establish a standard freemium tier, timed free production trial or published paid-pilot package.

evidence.note: Scope is Adyen for Platforms onboarding and UK payments pricing; negotiated pilot terms require separate confirmation.

examples.name: Chargebee — billing evaluation
examples.summary: Chargebee’s pricing page offers a free-trial signup alongside paid billing plans. Its Flow offer includes a usage charge even in the option with no monthly base fee.
examples.caveat: Confirm the current trial duration, enabled features and gateway charges during signup. The page does not justify assuming that production billing is free indefinitely.

evidence.note: Current pricing page checked 16 November 2026; no unsupported trial length or historical allowance is assumed.

examples.name: Paddle — free analytics alongside paid payments
examples.summary: Paddle advertises ProfitWell Metrics as free subscription analytics, including connections to other billing systems. Its payment sandbox is separate from live processing.
examples.caveat: Free analytics is a separate offer, not evidence of free merchant-of-record processing. A later sale of another product is cross-selling rather than a mandatory Metrics upgrade.

evidence.note: Free analytics, sandbox behavior and live commercial pricing are separately documented.
Entry-model definitions and domain fit are an analytical synthesis. The paid-pilot option is a proposed commercial design, not a verified standard vendor package.
